title: Goodbye — and the one farewell you shouldn't use
goal: Say goodbye, offer congratulations and good wishes, and keep a conversation going when a word escapes you — and learn the one Slovenian farewell that means "forever", which you must never say to a friend.
bekal: choosing a goodbye by how close you are: *čav*, *adijo*, *nasvidenje*, *se vidiva*
offering congratulations and wishes: *vse najboljše*, *srečno*, *veliko sreče*
rescuing a stalled conversation with six repair phrases

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na peronu
dialogs.intro: End of the semester. Budi is leaving for home from Ljubljana station. Maja and Eva see him off — and save him from one big mistake just in time.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: So you're off. When are you coming back?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pred pol leta nisem znal nič.
lines.id: Six months ago I didn't know anything.
lines.literal: before half of-year not-I-am known-m nothing.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Zdaj pa se pogovarjaš. To je vse.
lines.id: And now you can hold a conversation. That's what counts.
lines.literal: now but self you-converse. this is all.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: Don't! "Zbogom" is for the very last time.

notes: **Zbogom isn't just a more polite "goodbye".** It comes from *z Bogom* — "go with God" — and is used when people don't expect to meet again: a final farewell, a departure with no return, a death. Saying it to a friend you'll see next month sounds like announcing something terrible. For ordinary goodbyes, use *nasvidenje*, *adijo* or *se vidiva*.

**Nikar isn't the same as ne.** *Ne* negates; *nikar* gently forbids, roughly like "don't!" or "oh, don't". It almost always stands alone or before a command: *Nikar!*, *Nikar ne skrbi* (don't worry).

**Se pogovarjaš — this is the real measure.** Not how many tables you've memorized, but whether you can **hold a conversation**. After twenty units you can greet people, introduce yourself, order, shop, ask the way, tell the time, talk about yesterday and tomorrow, decline politely and explain that your head hurts. That's far more than enough for daily life.
**Pred pol leta and čez pol leta.** *Pred* points back, *čez* points forward — a pair of prepositions you met in unit 10. *Pred enim tednom* (a week ago), *čez en teden* (in a week).

**Upam** (I hope) is one word that rounds off lots of sentences warmly: *Upam, da se kmalu vidiva* (I hope we see each other soon), *Upam, da bo lepo* (I hope the weather's nice). Its partner is *Želim ti vse dobro* — I wish you all the best.

grammars.title: Pozdravi in voščila — goodbyes and good wishes
body: Slovenian goodbyes run from the most familiar to the most distant. The last row is the one you need to recognize but should not use.
after: The wishes you'll need most: **Vse najboljše!** (happy birthday — literally "all the best"), **Čestitam!** (congratulations, on an achievement), **Veliko sreče!** (good luck), **Vesel božič!** (Merry Christmas), **Srečno novo leto!** (Happy New Year), **Dober tek!** (enjoy your meal), **Na zdravje!** (cheers; also "bless you" when someone sneezes).
If someone says one of these to you, the answer that always works is **Hvala, enako!** — thanks, same to you.

grammars.title: The six cases in one table
body: Here is the whole Slovenian case system you've worked through unit by unit, stacked onto one page. The nouns: *knjiga* (feminine), *vlak* (masculine), *mesto* (neuter).
after: Notice how many boxes are **twins**: for *vlak*, four of the six sound like *vlak* or *vlaka*; for *mesto*, the accusative is identical to the basic form. A system that first looks like thirty-six forms really contains only a dozen or so different sounds.

The ones you truly need to master at A1 are just four: **imenovalnik** (the dictionary form), **tožilnik** (the object — *Pijem kavo*), **mestnik** (place — *V Ljubljani*) and **rodilnik** (negation and numbers — *Nimam časa*, *pet knjig*). The other two will come on their own with use.

blocks.text: Real conversations don't stall because you're short on grammar; they stall because one word goes missing and you stop. The sentences below are tools for **staying in the conversation** — and they're worth more than a hundred new words.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: How do you say … in Slovenian?
I don't speak it well yet.

blocks.text: The sentence *Se še učim slovensko* has an effect in Slovenia that's hard to overstate. Because few foreigners learn the language, saying it almost always changes the tone of the conversation: people slow down, correct you kindly, and often stay in Slovenian instead of switching to English — which is exactly what you need.

blocks.title: The rules that matter most
items: **Don't stop to correct yourself.** A finished sentence with a mistake is far more useful than a perfect one that never comes out.
**If you forget to change a noun's ending, let it go.** *Grem v Ljubljana* is still fully understood. What kills a conversation isn't the wrong case — it's silence.
**Say one Slovenian sentence to a real person every day.** Just one. That's what separates people who finish a course from people who can speak.

sections.title: Kaj pa zdaj? — after this course

blocks.text: You've just completed level A1: about 800 words, six cases, three tenses, and one antique called the dual (*dvojina*) that hardly any other language in the world still has.

What awaits you at A2 are the things this course deliberately simplified: the **conditional** with *bi* in full, **definite adjective forms** (*dober* versus *dobri*), the cases of **adjectives and pronouns** in all six forms, complex sentences with *ki* and *da*, and a second layer of vocabulary for work, health and official matters.

head: What you can do now
Example
rows: Say where you're from and where you live
Ask the way and the time
*Včeraj sem bil doma. Jutri bom delal.*

blocks.text: A few ways to keep going without a book: **RTV Slovenija** broadcasts daily news in simple Slovenian; **Slovenščina na daljavo** offers free online practice from the University of Ljubljana; and the **Center za slovenščino kot drugi in tuji jezik** runs official exams if you need one for work or a residence permit.

You're saying goodbye to your lecturer. ____

exercises.prompt: Wave review — unit 18. Translate into Slovenian without looking back at the unit.

answers: Adijo! — Nasvidenje! — Vse najboljše! — Veliko sreče! — Na zdravje! — Na zdravje!
Oprostite, ne razumem. — Lahko ponovite, prosim? — Prosim, počasneje. — Kaj pomeni vabilo? — Se še učim slovensko. — Prosim, napišite.
Kdaj se vrneš? — Čez pol leta. — Pogrešal bom Ljubljano. — Pred pol leta nisem znal nič. — Nasvidenje in srečno! — Hvala za vse.
Eno vozovnico do Bleda, prosim. — Kdaj gre vlak? — Koliko časa traja? — Potujem z avtobusom. — Srečno pot!
